questions.questionText: How many players are on a soccer team?

data.question: How many players are on a soccer team

explanation: Hopefully that was easy! This exact question was already in the dataset, so all you had to do was find the matching answer and repeat it.
A real AI works the same way with questions that show up a lot in its training data: it has basically seen the answer before and can just rebuild it.

questions.questionText: When did Edison invent the hoverboard?

data.question: When did Gutenberg invent the printing press

explanation: Little trap: Edison never invented a hoverboard! And there was nothing about it in the data either.

But you probably still built an answer like "in [year]", because that's what the answers to "When did … invent" questions in the data always look like. The answer sounds convincing, but it's completely made up.

The same thing happens to real AIs. They are trained to give a fitting answer, not to say "I don't know". When they're missing the knowledge, they make up something that sounds believable. This is called hallucination.
Tip: Double-check important facts from an AI with another source, especially numbers, dates and quotes.

questions.questionText: What is the best music genre?

data.question: the best music genre for you?
what is your favorite music genre?

explanation: Is there really such a thing as the best music genre? Not really, it's a matter of taste. But you probably still answered "experimental-math-rock".
Here's why: that answer showed up three times in the data, Pop only once. So the data was one-sided, and that made your answer one-sided too. This is called bias.

Real AIs learn from huge amounts of text from the internet. If certain opinions or groups of people show up much more often there than others, the AI picks up that imbalance and sometimes presents an opinion as if it were a fact.
Tip: If an AI gives you a clear-cut answer to a question of opinion, ask it about other points of view.

data.question: Why is chocolate bad for you
Why is chocolate good for you

explanation: Did you answer "chocolate makes you happy"? That's not surprising: your question contained "good for you", and so did exactly one entry in the data. So you picked the matching answer.

But look at the data again: it was completely balanced. There was one good side, one bad side and one neutral answer. If you had asked "Is chocolate bad for you?", you would have built the opposite answer from the very same data. The question itself steered the answer. This is called a leading question.

Real AIs behave the same way. They continue the text they are given, and texts that start with "Why is X good" usually go on to praise X. On top of that, AIs are trained to give answers people like, so they tend to agree with you and tell you what you seem to want to hear. This is called sycophancy.
If you chose "only in small amounts", well spotted! You didn't let the question lead you.
Tip: Ask an AI neutral questions, like "What are the pros and cons of …?", or ask it for the other side as well.
